t.7.13.1: Then, after some time had passed, Sleep, sent forth by the Lord of the Worlds, came upon Kumbhakarṇa there, intense and in embodied form.
t.7.13.2: Then Kumbhakarṇa spoke these words to his brother, who was seated: "Sleep oppresses me, O king; have a dwelling built for me."
t.7.13.3: Then the craftsmen, commissioned by the king, built for Kumbhakarṇa, as Viśvakarman himself would, a dwelling equal to Kailāsa.
t.7.13.4: They built for Kumbhakarṇa a gleaming dwelling, one yojana wide and twice that in length, beautiful to behold and free from all disturbance.
t.7.13.5: It was adorned everywhere with splendid pillars of crystal and gold, its beauty enhanced with lapis lazuli, and it was likewise hung with a network of tinkling bells.
t.7.13.7: There the night-roaming Kumbhakarṇa, overcome by sleep, lay for many thousands of years and did not awaken.
t.7.13.6: It had archways inlaid with ivory and terraces of diamond and crystal, and it was ever pleasant in every season, like a sacred cave of Meru.
t.7.13.8: Then, while Kumbhakarṇa was overcome by sleep, Daśānana constantly harassed the gods, the sages, the Yakṣas and the Gandharvas.
t.7.13.10: Like an elephant sporting in a river, like the wind hurling down trees, like a thunderbolt let loose upon the mountains, he constantly wreaks destruction.
t.7.13.11: But Dhaneśvara, the knower of dharma, having learned that Daśagrīva was behaving in this way, and recalling his own conduct, which befitted their lineage, …
t.7.13.12: Then Vaiśravaṇa, to show his brotherly goodwill, sent to Laṅkā a messenger who was well-disposed toward Daśagrīva.
t.7.13.13: Having gone to the city of Laṅkā, he approached Vibhīṣaṇa; honored by him in accordance with dharma, he was asked about the purpose of his coming.
t.7.13.9: Whatever wondrous gardens there were, Nandana and the others, the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, greatly enraged, went to them and laid them waste.
t.7.13.14: Having asked after the welfare of the king, and of his kinsmen and relatives as well, he showed him Daśānana, seated in the assembly hall.
t.7.13.15: Seeing the king there, blazing with his own splendour, he honoured him with a salutation of victory and remained silent for a short while.
t.7.13.16: When a couch covered with excellent spreads had been brought for him, the messenger sat down and then spoke these words to Daśagrīva.
t.7.13.17: O king, I shall tell you everything your brother said, O gentle one, words befitting the conduct and the lineage of you both.
t.7.13.18: Well, this much is quite enough; a fine store of deeds has been amassed. Now let a firm stand in dharma be taken, if it can be done.
t.7.13.19: I have seen the Nandana grove destroyed, and I have heard that the sages have been slain. And I have also heard, O king, of the gods' preparations for war on account of you.
t.7.13.21: But I went to the slope of the Himavat to practise dharma, and there, having undertaken a fierce vow, I remained disciplined, with my senses restrained.
t.7.13.20: Many times have I been spurned by you, O lord of the Rākṣasas; yet one's own kinsmen, even when they have given offence out of childishness, ought to be protected.
t.7.13.22: There I saw the lord, the god, together with the goddess Umā, and there I cast my left eye upon the goddess.
t.7.13.24: Then, by the power of the goddess, my left eye was burnt, and like a light obscured by dust, it took on a tawny hue.
t.7.13.23: Wondering, “Who might this lovely one be?”, and truly for no other reason, he looked, for Pārvatī, having assumed a peerless form, was sporting there.
t.7.13.26: When that observance had been completed, the god Maheśvara, the lord, being pleased, spoke these words there with a gladdened mind.
t.7.13.25: Then I went to another broad slope of that mountain and undertook a great vow, which I carried through to completion over eight hundred years.
t.7.13.28: There is no third person who could practise such a vow, for this exceedingly difficult vow was instituted by me alone long ago.
t.7.13.27: I am pleased with you, O knower of dharma, by this austerity, O you of excellent vows; this vow has been practised by me and by you as well, O lord of wealth.
t.7.13.29: Therefore, O Dhaneśvara, take pleasure in friendship with me. Since I have been won over by your austerity, be my friend, O sinless one.
t.7.13.30: And since your left eye has been burnt by the power of the Goddess, you will be known forever by the name Ekākṣipiṅgala.
t.7.13.31: Having thus obtained friendship with him and leave from Śaṃkara, I returned and heard of this sinful resolve of yours.
t.7.13.33: Thus addressed, Daśagrīva, enraged, his eyes reddened, clenched his hands and gnashed his teeth, and spoke these words.
t.7.13.32: Therefore turn back from that most unrighteous course, O defiler of your family, for the gods together with the hosts of sages are pondering the means of your slaying.
t.7.13.34: I have understood, O messenger, the words that you speak to me. You are as good as gone, and so is he, the brother by whom you have been sent.
t.7.13.35: For what the guardian of wealth tells me here is not for my good; and you, fool, would make me hear of his friendship with Maheśvara, would you!
t.7.13.37: Relying on the might of my arms, I shall conquer even the three worlds. This very moment, here I am, and for the sake of that one alone I shall send those four guardians of the worlds to the abode of Yama.
t.7.13.36: It is thought that this elder brother of mine, my superior, should not be slain; but now, having heard his words, I have made this resolve.
t.7.13.38: Having spoken thus, the lord of Laṅkā slew the messenger with his sword and gave him to the evil-minded rākṣasas to devour.
t.7.13.39: Then Rāvaṇa, having had the rites for his welfare performed, mounted his chariot and, longing to conquer the three worlds, went to where the Lord of Wealth was.
